hints: Notice the question says repeated measurements of a fixed quantity are averaged - think about how the readings spread around the true value.
Recall that random error changes unpredictably from reading to reading, while systematic error shifts every reading in the same direction by a similar amount.
Ask what happens to positive and negative random deviations when you add them in a mean, and whether the same cancellation can happen to a one-sided systematic shift.
walkthrough: Identify the situation: several readings of the same fixed quantity are taken, then the mean is calculated to give a best value.
State the rule for random error: it causes unpredictable scatter, with some readings too high and some too low due to factors like reaction time or electrical noise.
Explain the averaging effect on random error: in the sum for the mean, the high and low deviations partly cancel, so the mean is closer to the true value and random error is reduced.
State the rule for systematic error: it is a consistent offset in one direction, for example a zero error or badly calibrated instrument affecting every reading the same way.
Conclude that averaging cannot remove this constant offset because every value in the mean carries the same shift, so systematic error is unaffected. This is option C.

options.A: Averaging does not remove a consistent shift, so systematic error is not reduced by taking a mean.
options.B: Averaging does reduce the scatter from random error because high and low readings partly cancel.
options.C: Random readings spread above and below the true value cancel in the mean, while a systematic shift affects every reading equally and remains.
options.D: This reverses the physics: averaging helps random error, not the constant offset of systematic error.
